newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-DAVIS CUP STIRS EMOTIONS AND REVIVES MEMORIES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-DAVIS CUP STIRS EMOTIONS AND REVIVES MEMORIES.

text.p: When Henri Cochet hit the winning shot to bring France their first Davis Cup in 1927, his wife swooned at the side of the court.
News of the famous victory in Philadelphia over the almighty Americans brought Parisians on to the streets in a frenzy of dancing, singing and celebration.
Much the same happened in 1991, when France won the trophy after a gap of 59 years and against all the odds by beating the United States in Lyon.
Players wept, captain Yannick Noah led supporters round the court in an ecstatic conga and France erupted in an orgy of joy and congratulation.
Not just French emotions run high at Davis Cup time. Even the normally phlegmatic Swedes, who meet France in this year's final starting on Friday, can get excited.

Bjorn Borg was flung repeatedly into the air after he led Sweden to their first win in 1975. The country then turned tennis mad. Thousands signed up at clubs and local councils the length of the country set about building courts to cater for the new passion.
Professional tennis is essentially a lonely and obsessive pursuit. Players travel the world seeking individual glory and wealth, knowing success depends on their own effort.

A team competiton such as the Davis Cup comes as a shock with the intensity of its shared highs and lows. International footballers know all about team spirit and patriotic fervour. But, in much the same way as the Ryder Cup makes grown golfers cry, so the Davis cup does strange things to tennis players.
"This is the most wonderful day of my life," Guy Forget gushed after France's 1991 triumph. His normally voluble team mate Henri Leconte was speechless, tears streaming down his face.

In his "Story of the Davis Cup", Australian tennis writer Alan Trengrove tells how the normally cool Arthur Ashe, then U.S. captain, broke down while speaking at a Davis Cup celebration dinner in 1981 as he reminisced about his experiences in the competition.
Ashe said the highlight of his career was not becoming the first black man to win Wimbledon but helping to lift the Davis Cup in 1968.

It was not as if an American triumph was in any way unusual. The United States won the first competition in 1900 and have taken home the trophy 30 times since. Australia have won it 26 times with Britain way back in third place on nine. France and Sweden lie in fourth and fifth places with seven and five wins respectively.
The Davis Cup has undergone many revisions, most notably in 1973 when the competiton was belatedly opened up to professionals and in 1981 when prize money was introduced.

It has survived pauses during two world wars and countless political crises. During the 1970s the inclusion of apartheid South Africa provoked violent demonstrations and several walkouts culminating in India refusing to play the 1974 final and allowing South Africa a walkover victory. South Africa was eventually barred between 1978 and 1992.
The Cup has also survived all manner of gamesmanship, particularly where choice of surface is concerned, crowd violence, player histrionics and fights on court.
Earlier this year, Austria's Thomas Muster stalked off court in Brazil saying he would not put up with the crowd's abuse. Austria forfeited the tie.
Muster's complaint was not unprecedented.

At the 1914 final, Australians were horrified at the partisan behaviour of the U.S. crowd who flung bottles across the court, yelled abuse at officials who judged points in the visitors' favour and applauded every Australian mistake. The Australians still won the Cup.

Paraguayan ties also have a reputation for being lively. In 1985 during matches against France spectators constantly interrupted play, line judges were accused of making obscene gestures at players, fights broke out and a French journalist was knocked unconscious. But the tie was completed with Paraguay the victors and rules concerning disruptions were tightened up the following year.

Players' antics can on occasion be more disruptive than the crowd's. John McEnroe, a passionate supporter of the Davis Cup was, nevertheless, no better behaved playing for his country than on the tour. He was always arguing with opponents and officials and even with his own captain Ashe, who told him during a particularly bad-tempered semifinal in 1981 that he would concede the tie rather than have the referee disqualify a U.S. player.
The entertaining but notoriously irascible Ilie Nastase was disqualified after attempting to thump Britain's David Lloyd over the head with his racket during a tie in Bucharest in 1977.
Trengrove cites Nastase as one of the players who found the responsibility of Davis Cup an incredible strain, particularly at home.
"You want to win so much for the people that every shot you miss is like an arrow straight to your heart," the Romanian said.
